entry.title: What comes after lithium-ion batteries? | with Saiful Islam

media:group.media:title: What comes after lithium-ion batteries? | with Saiful Islam
media:group.media:description:
Will your next phone, car or home battery still rely on lithium-ion? Materials chemist Prof Saiful Islam explores the batteries and solar cells driving the energy transition, from lithium-ion and sodium-ion to solid-state batteries and perovskite solar cells, with a few Ri style explosions along the way.
Ten years after his Christmas Lectures (and that world record lemon battery), Saiful explains how supercomputer modelling, working hand in hand with experiments, is helping design better energy materials atom by atom. He looks at how electric vehicles and solar power have grown since 2016, and what could come next.
Join this channel as a member to watch the exclusive scientist Q&A every week: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCYeF244yNGuFefuFKqxIAXw/join
Subscribe for regular science videos: http://bit.ly/RiSubscRibe _____ In this lecture: • How lithium ions move through a battery, and why it matters for charging speed • Why researchers are moving away from cobalt, and what lithium-rich cathodes could offer • Sodium vs lithium: pros, cons and a live reaction with water • Solid-state batteries and super-ionic conductors • Perovskite solar cells: rapid efficiency gains, but can they last? • The surge in global solar capacity _____ Chapters: 0:00 Why new materials matter for energy 3:05 Energy vs power: Faraday's candle and an explosive demo 7:28 Crystals, ion conduction and modelling materials with supercomputers 13:34 Lithium-ion batteries and the electric vehicle boom 18:26 Inside a lithium-ion battery: how lithium ions move 25:10 Future cathodes: lithium-rich materials and recycling 30:03 Sodium-ion vs lithium: audience face-off and alkali metals in water 37:42 Solid-state batteries and super-ionic conductors 39:53 Christmas Lectures 2016 and the world record lemon battery 45:26 Perovskite solar cells vs silicon 53:17 The solar boom: terawatts and developing countries 54:57 Hydrogen, a Tesla coil finale and the future of green energy _____ ABOUT THE SPEAKER Saiful Islam is Professor of Materials Science at the University of Oxford and presented the 80th TV anniversary Royal Institution Christmas Lectures in 2016 on the theme of energy, which included a world record lemon battery. His research encompasses materials for batteries and solar cells, and he has been involved with Faraday Institution projects on lithium batteries. entry.title: What Star Trek got right about science (and what it got wrong) | Part 2

media:group.media:title: What Star Trek got right about science (and what it got wrong) | Part 2
media:group.media:description:
What would it actually take to become a Starfleet officer? How close are we to replicators, warp drive and futuristic medical technology? And what does real plasma have to do with a phaser?
In Part 2 of The science of Star Trek, reserve astronaut Meganne Christian takes us inside real astronaut training and explores how today's space technology compares with the world of Star Trek. Discover how astronauts prepare for microgravity, how 3D printing could transform medicine in space, and how scientists are already manufacturing materials and pharmaceuticals in orbit.
We then return to the Royal Institution's own history, exploring the surprising connections between scientific discoveries made here and technologies imagined in Star Trek — from wireless communication and robotics to holograms and artificial intelligence. The event concludes with live demonstrations exploring plasma, Tesla coils and the science behind Star Trek's spectacular effects.
This is Part 2 of a two-part event. Watch Part 1 first for the full story of the science behind Star Trek: https://youtu.be/y4szgt79BX8
Filmed at the Royal Institution in London on 12 September 2026.
Viewer note: Actor Martin Quinn has requested that his section of the talk be edited out of the YouTube video. entry.title: How maths reveals what your brain hides | with Kit Yates

media:group.media:title: How maths reveals what your brain hides | with Kit Yates
media:group.media:description:
Why do some people see a white and gold dress, while others see blue and black? And how can a coin flip help us uncover what people won’t admit to in a survey?
Mathematician Kit Yates explores how our understanding of the world is shaped as much by missing information as by what’s there. Through illusions, live demos and gripping real-world stories, he introduces three types of “missingness”:
• Intrinsic: how our senses and brains filter, fill in and distort reality • Extrinsic: how bias, bad polls and filtered data hide the truth before it reaches us • Constructive: how absence itself can be evidence, from Sherlock Holmes to the coelacanth
Kit’s book, You Don’t Know What You’re M ss ng, is available here: https://geni.us/kSBlAbl
This was filmed at the Royal Institution on the 19th of September 2026.
Subscribe for regular science videos: http://bit.ly/RiSubscRibe
The Ri is a charity. Become a channel member to support our content AND unlock exclusive Q&As with our scientists: https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCYeF244yNGuFefuFKqxIAXw/join _____________________ Kit Yates is an author, broadcaster and academic specialising in the role of mathematics in everyday life. He completed his PhD in mathematics at the University of Oxford and is now Professor of Mathematical Biology and Public Engagement at the University of Bath. He is the author of three books: The Maths of Life and Death (a Sunday Times Science Book of the Year) and now How to Expect the Unexpected and You Don’t Know What You’re M ss ng, and is a prominent commentator on the role of mathematics/science in society writing regularly for the Guardian, the Independent, BBC Futures and a range of other media outlets. He regularly appears on radio shows like the BBC’s More or Less, and Inside Science as well as on TV news, current affairs shows and documentaries. ______________ Chapters: 0:00 Welcome: what is "missingness"? 2:40 Reading tests: how your brain fills in the gaps 8:12 Why perception isn't objective reality 13:01 Why a metal spoon feels colder than a wooden one 15:08 Sensory adaptation (and a deadly gas leak) 19:27 Inattentional blindness: the card trick 23:36 Duck-rabbit and The Dress: why we see different colours 29:23 Anguish Languish and the Stroop effect 35:10 Selection bias: how polls mislead us 45:11 Response bias: why people don't tell the truth 49:13 Live maths game: the randomised response trick 57:13 Sherlock Holmes and the power of absent evidence 1:03:59 The Wason card test and the scientific method
